This page sets out the whole exercise. The [case study](index.qmd) presents the original study, the Multi100 project and the five reanalyses in full, and it is the place to start if you have not read it. The one-day formats of the course work mainly in the [Browser lab](lab.qmd), which runs the exercise in a browser tab with the data in place, and the workspace that you download and open in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) is the option for those who have installed R; the three-day course works in the workspace. Both give the same numbers. Come back here whenever you want the overview again.

---

## The claim you are working on

Five independent analysts reanalysed a claim made by the original author (OA) as part of the Multi100 project. The claim, as presented to all analysts, was:

> "…poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016, p. 619)

The published coefficient – the specific number that the Task 2 constraints pointed to – is:

> **Unemployment → cosmopolitan EU framing: b = −0.0034, t = −4.03, p < .001** (Table 3, Model 1)

This comes from a three-level random-intercept model using pooled Eurobarometer data (16 waves, 2004–2013, 27 EU countries). Your first job is to reproduce one of the results that Multi100 recorded for this claim, choosing among the three that rest on aggregate data (Task 3). On the methods day your second job is to deviate from the reproduced specification – deliberately, with a written justification – and see what that does to the estimate; on the open-science day it is to plan a replication of the analysis that you reproduced.

---

## Which claim, and why {#which-claim}

The claim on the card is one of several that the paper makes. The SCORE programme selected claims from published abstracts, and the sentence it took from this paper is the first half of a two-part hypothesis. In the paper itself, that hypothesis reads: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" (p. 621). The second sentence, which compares two of the four framing scales with the other two, was not part of the claim given to the analysts, and neither was the second hypothesis of the paper, about the gap between high- and low-educated citizens, which the [individual-level module](../../companion/individual-level.qmd#sec-claim2) takes up. The Multi100 project then narrowed the card further in its constrained phase, fixing the cosmopolitan scale as the outcome and the unemployment rate as the predictor, which is why the coefficient above is the one with which the five results were to be compared.

Each of those steps was a decision that someone other than you made, and each one shaped what "replicating the claim" could mean. Testing the first sentence needs one outcome and one predictor. Testing the second needs a grouping of the scales, and the [measurement module](../../companion/measurement.qmd#sec-theory) shows that the data only half support that grouping. The education hypothesis needs the respondents rather than the country-years. Choosing which sentence to replicate is the first specification decision of any replication, and it is made before the estimand, the graph or the menu, usually by the people who wrote the card. The course keeps to the card, so that its results can be set beside those of the five analysts.

## The five Multi100 analysts {#the-five-published-analysts}

Before you begin, here is what the five Multi100 analysts found when they reanalysed the same claim, as Multi100 recorded it:

| Analyst | Tool | Statistic | N | Partial r, recorded | Reproduced in the browser lab |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 018OL | R | t = −1.21 | 420 | −0.060 | yes, on its 420 cells |
| C6HJR | R | t = −3.80 | 270 | −0.242 | yes, on the course panel |
| KEVF1 | R | t = −5.90 | 209,826 | −0.452 | no – needs the respondent files |
| KQXUE | Stata | t = −7.17 | 270 | −0.419 | yes, on its 270 country-years |
| PRL47 | Stata | z = −3.59 | 394,575 | −0.006 | no – needs the respondent files |

All five reported a negative effect, in the direction of the original. The recorded partial correlations range from −0.006 to −0.452, a factor of nearly 80, but most of that spread comes from the conversion of each test statistic into a correlation rather than from the analyses themselves. PRL47 and C6HJR report almost the same statistic, yet the z of PRL47 was converted on the number of respondents, which pulls any correlation towards zero. Section 4 of the [case study](index.qmd#sec-recorded) shows how the conversion works, and the [Multiverse page](multiverse.qmd#reference-marks) places each result on the degrees of freedom of its own inference. The last column says which results the browser lab and the workspace reproduce: the three that rest on means of countries or of cells. The other two fitted their models on respondents, whose files only a GESIS account can give, and the three-day course, which builds the respondent file from the downloads of the participants, reproduces them too.

---

## The tasks

The exercise has five numbered tasks, and each format of the course takes the ones that it can finish: the open-science and data-tools days end after Task 3, the open-science day then writing a preregistration for a replication that is not run, and the methods day runs all five. The page of each track says which tasks fall in which part. Each task below says what to do in the browser lab and, where it differs, in the workspace; both give the same numbers.

### Task 1 – Get yourself running

The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. *Browser lab:* wait for the engine to finish downloading, then run the setup-check cell and confirm that the panel has 270 rows. The vocabulary warm-up on the same page – three Rs and one impostor – is there to fill the waiting. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE, run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, and render the report skeleton once. If your installation will not cooperate, do not fight it, because the browser lab holds every task.

### Task 2 – Meet the panel, name the estimand, draw the graph

The task has three parts, taken in order. First, look at the data. The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the exercise, 270 country-years with unemployment and GDP growth alongside several EU-framing measures. It is published in the main folder of the OSF fork that its analyst maintains (`osf.io/6zqct`), while the official Multi100 archival record is at `osf.io/8rtwe`. Run the small-multiples figure and find the countries that move sharply around 2009, because the fixed-effects models use that variation within countries.

Second, write the **estimand statement**: the unit-specific quantity, the target population, the aggregation. The template gives you the structure, and filling it in makes you say precisely what this claim is about.

Third, complete the **causal graph**. Take the `#` off the arrows you are willing to defend, run `adjustmentSets()` again, and check which adjustment set the graph now implies; then write two sentences for your notes on what two-way fixed effects adjust for and what they cannot fix. *Browser lab:* the graph is built with `dagify()`, and `adjustmentSets()` prints the answer that dagitty gives for each combination of the arrows in the cell, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty. *Workspace:* edit `R/dag_starter.R`, where dagitty answers for any graph. The [causal-graphs companion module](../../companion/dags.qmd) works the material through slowly. On the open-science and data-tools days the graph is optional.

### Task 3 – Reproduce a recorded result

Choose one of the three analysts whose results rest on aggregate data, and refit the analysis until the value on record comes back to the third decimal. This is the reproduction step, in which the same data and the same model give the same number.

| Analyst | Data | Model | On record |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | `EUframes_cy.csv`, 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year, conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df |
| 018OL | `analyst_018OL.csv`, 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom | t = −1.206 on 396.9 df |

The panel of C6HJR is the course panel. The files of KQXUE and 018OL were rebuilt by the course from the sixteen GESIS waves, following the code that each analyst deposited on the OSF (osf.io/vycgd and osf.io/nz7ka) step by step, slips included, and their [codebook](data/analyst_panels_codebook.md) says how. The Stata code of KQXUE appended the wave EB 62.0 twice, and the files of 018OL put the wave EB 79.3, fielded in 2013, in 2012. *Browser lab:* each analyst has an exercise cell of its own, with gaps to fill, a hint and a full solution, and the first run of the cell of 018OL downloads the packages for mixed models, about 32 MB. *Workspace:* the three reproductions are written out in the working script and in Task 3 of the report. In class, type the analyst and the value into the chat, for example `KQXUE t = -7.169`, hold it, and send it when the facilitator says go.

The two analysts who worked on respondents, KEVF1 and PRL47, need the respondent files, which only a GESIS account can give; the three-day course reproduces them from the downloads of the participants. The paper itself was also put through attempts at reproduction and replication in the SCORE programme, which section 2 of the [case study](index.qmd#sec-repetition) describes.

### Task 4 – Work the menu

This task is **exploratory**, and it belongs to the methods day. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](menu.qmd), see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision, and every argument defaults to the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR on which the menu and the curve are built, so changing one thing means changing one argument. An option that is off the curve, such as pooled OLS (`estimator = "pooled_cl"`), stops with the reason why and the page of the course that teaches it. `my_experiments()` prints everything you have tried, side by side – the small multiverse that you have just built. Then pick the one you would defend if you had to, and `submit_exploration()` puts it on the live [Multiverse](multiverse.qmd) chart as an **exploratory** result.

Nothing in this task is preregistered. You are allowed to look, change your mind and try again, and the chart labels the result as exploratory for that reason.

### Task 5 – Declare one specification, run it, report it

The class first reads its exploratory results on the class chart, laid over the curve of 864 specifications: which decisions move the result most, where the five reanalyses and the original study sit on the main chart, and **your own placement**, the share of the 864 specifications that lie further in the direction of the claim than the estimate you submitted. The [reading on the specification curve](reading-inference.qmd) is the companion for this part.

Then pick ONE specification from the curve, one option for each of the fourteen decisions on the menu, and complete the preregistration block **before you run that specification**. It is a shortened but real preregistration template: what you are testing, what you already know about the data, your one specification, why those controls (grounded in your Task 2 graph), and the rule by which you will judge the result. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the convention of the course and is applied for you. The claim expects framing to rise with growth, so the sign of a growth slope is flipped, and 'supports the claim' then reads as a negative sign for every specification.

Run `prereg()` once the block is complete and before you write the model code below it. On the browser lab page, copy the block into your notes; in the workspace, the rendered report, which carries the date on which it was rendered, keeps the declaration above the cells that fit the specification. Then translate the declaration into model syntax yourself – `build_model()` accepts only code that matches what you declared – run it, and `report_result()` prints a one-click, pre-filled form link. Your submission appears on the chart as a **declared** result beside the exploratory ones.

Task 4 and Task 5 run identical code. What separates them is that an exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit twice so that the two sets of results can be compared side by side.

---

## What counts as a result {#what-makes-a-result-valid}

On the methods day, your result is valid for the multiverse chart if it:

- is one of the 864 specifications on the curve, so that it reports the coefficient on the predictor that measures economic performance (unemployment or GDP growth, in one of its published series and forms) from a model of the country-year panel,
- is submitted to the class-results form via the `report_result()` link (so that it appears on the live [Multiverse](multiverse.qmd) chart), and
- has a written justification for the choice you made (2 sentences is enough).

The whole exercise depends on the justification. Auspurg & Brüderl (2021) argue that a multiverse of unjustified specifications shows dispersion and nothing more; the stated reasons are what let it count as evidence.
